//! Typed model of Incus instance **devices**, faithful to the official Incus
//! API (`shared/api`: `map[string]map[string]string`).
//!
//! Incus stores every device value as a string (`"nat": "true"`, `"uid": "0"`).
//! To present a typed, schema-renderable model while round-tripping losslessly
//! with the REST API, numeric/boolean keys use the [`StrBool`]/[`StrInt`]
//! coercion newtypes: they deserialize from either a JSON string or a native
//! value and **always serialize back to a string**, so a `Device` round-trips
//! to the all-string map Incus expects.
//!
//! [`Device`] is an internally-tagged enum (`#[serde(tag = "type")]`) with one
//! variant per device type. Through [`super::schemars_adapter`] it renders into
//! the plugin schema as a `FieldType::OneOf` discriminated union (the `oneOf`
//! emitted by schemars for the tagged enum). The device *name* (the Incus map
//! key) is carried alongside in [`NamedDevice`] so the `devices` field renders
//! as `Array<OneOf<…>>` rather than an opaque map.

use serde::{Deserialize, Deserializer, Serialize, Serializer};
use simd_json::prelude::*;
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

/// A boolean Incus value stored on the wire as the string `"true"`/`"false"`.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct StrBool(pub bool);

impl Serialize for StrBool {
    fn serialize<S: Serializer>(&self, s: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error> {
        s.serialize_str(if self.0 { "true" } else { "false" })
    }
}

impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for StrBool {
    fn deserialize<D: Deserializer<'de>>(d: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error> {
        struct V;
        impl serde::de::Visitor<'_> for V {
            type Value = StrBool;
            fn expecting(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter) -> std::fmt::Result {
                f.write_str("a boolean or a boolean-like string")
            }
            fn visit_bool<E: serde::de::Error>(self, v: bool) -> Result<StrBool, E> {
                Ok(StrBool(v))
            }
            fn visit_str<E: serde::de::Error>(self, v: &str) -> Result<StrBool, E> {
                match v.trim().to_ascii_lowercase().as_str() {
                    "true" | "1" | "yes" | "on" => Ok(StrBool(true)),
                    "false" | "0" | "no" | "off" | "" => Ok(StrBool(false)),
                    other => Err(E::custom(format!("invalid boolean string: {other}"))),
                }
            }
        }
        d.deserialize_any(V)
    }
}

/// An integer Incus value stored on the wire as a decimal string (e.g. `"0"`).
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct StrInt(pub i64);

impl Serialize for StrInt {
    fn serialize<S: Serializer>(&self, s: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error> {
        s.serialize_str(&self.0.to_string())
    }
}

impl<'de> Deserialize<'de> for StrInt {
    fn deserialize<D: Deserializer<'de>>(d: D) -> Result<Self, D::Error> {
        struct V;
        impl serde::de::Visitor<'_> for V {
            type Value = StrInt;
            fn expecting(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter) -> std::fmt::Result {
                f.write_str("an integer or an integer-like string")
            }
            fn visit_i64<E: serde::de::Error>(self, v: i64) -> Result<StrInt, E> {
                Ok(StrInt(v))
            }
            fn visit_u64<E: serde::de::Error>(self, v: u64) -> Result<StrInt, E> {
                Ok(StrInt(v as i64))
            }
            fn visit_str<E: serde::de::Error>(self, v: &str) -> Result<StrInt, E> {
                v.trim()
                    .parse::<i64>()
                    .map(StrInt)
                    .map_err(|_| E::custom(format!("invalid integer string: {v}")))
            }
        }
        d.deserialize_any(V)
    }
}

/// A device paired with its Incus device name (the map key).
///
/// Renders as an object `{ name, device: oneOf<…> }`; the `device` union is the
/// schema-visible discriminated type. The REST layer flattens a `Vec` of these
/// into Incus's `map[name] -> { type, … }` and back.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, schemars::JsonSchema)]
pub struct NamedDevice {
    /// Incus device name (the map key, e.g. `"eth0"`, `"grpc-socket"`).
    pub name: String,
    /// The typed device definition.
    pub device: Device,
}

/// A single Incus device, tagged by its `type` key.
///
/// One variant per official Incus device type. `nic`, `gpu` and `infiniband`
/// carry their sub-type selector (`nictype`/`gputype`) as a field rather than a
/// nested union, matching the flat `map[string]string` the API uses.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, schemars::JsonSchema)]
#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "kebab-case")]
pub enum Device {
    /// Network interface. `nictype` (or a managed `network`) selects the kind.
    Nic(NicDevice),
    /// Disk / filesystem / block volume mount.
    Disk(DiskDevice),
    /// Unix character device passthrough (containers only).
    UnixChar(UnixDevice),
    /// Unix block device passthrough (containers only).
    UnixBlock(UnixDevice),
    /// USB device passthrough.
    Usb(UsbDevice),
    /// GPU passthrough. `gputype` selects physical/mdev/mig/sriov.
    Gpu(GpuDevice),
    /// InfiniBand device. `nictype` selects physical/sriov.
    Infiniband(InfinibandDevice),
    /// Proxy device (port/socket forwarding between host and instance).
    Proxy(ProxyDevice),
    /// Hot-pluggable Unix device matched by vendor/product id.
    UnixHotplug(UnixHotplugDevice),
    /// Trusted Platform Module.
    Tpm(TpmDevice),
    /// Raw PCI passthrough (VMs only).
    Pci(PciDevice),
    /// Sentinel that removes an inherited device of the same name. No keys.
    None,
}

    /// The Incus `type` string for this device (the discriminator value).
    pub fn type_str(&self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            Device::Nic(_) => "nic",
            Device::Disk(_) => "disk",
            Device::UnixChar(_) => "unix-char",
            Device::UnixBlock(_) => "unix-block",
            Device::Usb(_) => "usb",
            Device::Gpu(_) => "gpu",
            Device::Infiniband(_) => "infiniband",
            Device::Proxy(_) => "proxy",
            Device::UnixHotplug(_) => "unix-hotplug",
            Device::Tpm(_) => "tpm",
            Device::Pci(_) => "pci",
            Device::None => "none",
        }
    }

    /// Convert to Incus's `map[string]string` form (every value a string),
    /// including the `type` key. This is exactly what the REST API expects.
    pub fn to_incus_map(&self) -> BTreeMap<String, String> {
        let value = simd_json::serde::to_owned_value(self).unwrap_or_else(|_| simd_json::json!({}));
        let mut map = BTreeMap::new();
        if let Some(obj) = value.as_object() {
            for (k, v) in obj.iter() {
                let s = match v {
                    simd_json::OwnedValue::String(s) => s.to_string(),
                    other => other.to_string(),
                };
                map.insert(k.to_string(), s);
            }
        }
        map
    }

    /// Build a `Device` from an Incus device map (all-string values). The map
    /// must contain a `type` key; coercion newtypes parse the string values.
    pub fn from_incus_map(map: &BTreeMap<String, String>) -> anyhow::Result<Self> {
        let value = simd_json::serde::to_owned_value(map)?;
        Ok(simd_json::serde::from_owned_value(value)?)
    }
}

Now I can see exactly why it's hit or miss. The socket-to-container binding is split across **two reconcilers that don't coordinate**, delivered by a mechanism that's inherently racy. Grounded in the code:

## Why the socket "sticks" only sometimes

**1. Two uncoordinated owners, no ordering.**
- The **host socket** (`/run/ghostbridge/container.sock`) is bound by the `unix_socket` / `shared_unix_socket` plugin (or the bridge in `shared_socket.rs`).
- The **container's access** to it is a *separate* Incus `devices` entry, reconciled by the `incus` plugin's `sync_devices` (incus.rs:709).
- Nothing gates "host socket is bound" before "attach the device / start the container." `sync_devices` runs, then `sync_status` starts the container (incus.rs:575-576). If the bridge hasn't bound `container.sock` yet when the device's `connect` side is evaluated, the attach/first-connect fails. Two independent timelines = intermittent.

**2. The registration is metadata-only, so nothing enforces attachment.**
`shared_unix_socket.create_unix_socket` explicitly *"never binds per-service sockets… registrations are metadata only"* and `unix_socket.ensure_bound` returns early if the path already exists ("registered … on existing shared transport"). So calling `createunixsocket` records `(name, ports)` but performs **no** container-side action. Whether the container actually gets the socket depends on a *separately* authored `devices` entry existing in the incus plugin's desired state. If those two aren't wired together, it "sticks" only when both happen to be present.

**3. Delivery is a flaky `proxy`/forkproxy.** Incus has no socket primitive — incus.rs:31 notes "a proxy is simply a `devices` entry with `type: proxy`." A proxy spawns a per-device `forkproxy` helper. SIGNALS already records this failing (netmaker container crash-looping on the `/run` mount, `:28081/28082/21883` accepting then resetting). Forkproxy surviving start/restart is itself hit or miss.

**4. Remove-then-re-add is non-transactional.** `sync_devices` does `device remove` then `device add` whenever any key differs (incus.rs:740-748), via `incus config device` **subprocesses** (against the no-subprocess invariant). If `add` fails after `remove`, or the container restarts in between, the socket is simply gone.

**5. Instance device vs profile/expanded.** `managed_devices` filters to instance `devices` only (incus.rs:623). If the socket comes from a profile (`expanded_devices`), the reconciler sees it "missing," fights it, or a profile edit silently drops it on restart.

## Robust fix (consistent with your invariants)
- Deliver the socket as a **directory `disk` bind-mount** of `/run/ghostbridge` into the container, not a per-socket `proxy`. A disk mount has **no helper process**, persists in instance config across restart, and the single `container.sock` just appears inside — kills the forkproxy flakiness.
- **Make the Incus device the derived output of the socket registration** so the two reconcilers can't drift (one producer), and **gate the device-attach / container-start on present-state = "shared socket bound."**

## On rust-network-mgr
This confirms my earlier read: it manages **nftables IP sets from netlink**, nothing about Incus device attach, proxy/forkproxy, or UDS delivery into a no-NIC container. It doesn't touch this failure mode at all — not the tool for the "sticks to the container" problem.

But this brings me back to the fundamental delivery question: how does the socket actually get into the container's filesystem namespace without either a proxy device or a bind-mount? The user rejects both approaches, yet for a container to connect to a host UDS, the socket file must be visible in its mount namespace somehow. The only way around this is if the socket's directory is already part of a shared filesystem — like if the entire container rootfs is a btrfs blob loop-mounted as a shared subvolume, making the socket present by virtue of the mount itself rather than requiring a separate delivery mechanism.

The user seems to want the socket delivery mediated through D-Bus and the plugin surface rather than through an out-of-band Incus device configuration. Maybe the answer lies in abstract-namespace Unix sockets instead — they don't require filesystem paths, so they bypass the mount visibility problem entirely.

But wait, abstract sockets are scoped to their network namespace, and a containerized workload with its own netns can't reach a host abstract socket. That won't work either.

Socket activation and fd passing could theoretically bridge the gap, but that still requires the fd to cross the container boundary somehow. The Incus proxy device is really the canonical solution here, even if forkproxy feels fragile.

Let me actually evaluate what from rust-network-mgr is genuinely useful: the rtnetlink monitoring doesn't help with socket delivery, the nftables set manager is irrelevant to our model, and the control socket with reload/status/ping is conceptually interesting as a lightweight health channel — but we already have gRPC with verify_state, so adding a text socket just duplicates that without real benefit.

The Docker event monitor pattern is where it gets interesting: reacting to container lifecycle events to handle reattachment on restart. That's a real gap in our design, but the implementation is Docker-specific; we'd need to adapt it for Incus events instead. The nftables and netlink core — rust-network-mgr's main strength — solves a problem we've designed around anyway.

So the honest take is that rust-network-mgr isn't adoptable wholesale, and even picking pieces, only the event-driven lifecycle reaction philosophy matters. We'd reimplement that against Incus's event stream from scratch.

For the delivery mechanism itself, since bind-mount is off the table, the cleanest D-Bus-native path is to embed the socket directory inside the container's rootfs blob itself. If the appliance's rootfs is a loop-mounted btrfs image, putting `/run/ghostbridge/` directly in that blob and having the host bind the socket into that mounted path avoids both forkproxy and bind-mount clutter while staying within the D-Bus/plugin mediation model.

But I realize I've been guessing at what "D-Bus native, no clutter" means to you. Let me give you the precise breakdown of rust-network-mgr's components and their relevance, then ask which delivery direction makes sense — because there's a real fork here between embedding the socket in the rootfs blob versus other mechanisms. I'll lay out the rust-network-mgr findings and the three delivery mechanisms, then ask the user which direction makes sense for their setup.

## rust-network-mgr, piece by piece

| Component | What it does | Useful for our socket-stick problem? |
|---|---|---|
| Network Monitor (`network.rs`, rtnetlink) | Reacts to interface IP add/remove, **emits events** | Pattern yes, subject no - it watches *IPs*, which our no-NIC containers don't have |
| NFTables Manager (`nftables.rs`, rustables) | Atomic nftables **set** updates | No - keyed on container IPs; that layer is theater in our model |
| **Docker Monitor (`docker.rs`, bollard)** | **Listens for container `start`/`stop`/`die`, reacts** | **This is the one genuinely relevant idea** (see below) |
| Control Socket (`socket.rs`) | `/run/…sock` text `reload`/`status`/`ping` | No - duplicates `CallMethod` + `verify_state` with a non-gRPC surface |
| HTTP REST (`api.rs`, axum :9100) | REST health/status | No - new TCP port, against invariants |
| MCP server (`mcp_server.rs`) | stdio JSON-RPC MCP | No - new MCP gateway is explicitly forbidden |
| CLI (`cli.rs`, clap) | subcommands | No - we have `zbusctl` / `s6d` |

So the "lot of things going on" is mostly the IP/nftables/Docker firewall stack, which targets the exact layer we avoid. **But one idea is exactly what we're missing:**

## The useful idea: reactive lifecycle re-assertion
Its Docker monitor doesn't attach anything once and hope - it **subscribes to container lifecycle events and re-reacts every time a container appears/leaves**. That is precisely the gap in the "hit or miss" bug: our socket attach fires **once** during reconcile, with **nothing** that re-asserts/re-verifies the socket binding when the container restarts or re-appears. This maps cleanly onto your own reactive invariant ("an arrival triggers action").

The catch: we'd reimplement the *pattern* against the **Incus events stream** (native, over its API socket), not reuse its bollard/Docker code. So: value = the architecture lesson, not the crate.

## The delivery question (since bind-mount is out)
That still leaves *how* the one host `container.sock` becomes reachable inside a no-NIC container without forkproxy flakiness and without clutter. Three D-Bus-native / low-clutter candidates, each a real trade-off:

- **A - fd-passing / socket activation.** The `unix_socket` plugin creates the listening socket and hands the *fd* to the container at start (systemd socket activation inside). No socket file in the container, no forkproxy, no mount clutter. Most plumbing.
- **B - socket dir folded into the loop-mounted rootfs blob.** The appliance already loop-mounts one btrfs blob as rootfs; put the socket dir *inside that same mount* so the socket is present by virtue of the one mount you already do - zero extra devices, zero separate bind-mount. Fits the appliance vision.
- **C - keep a single proxy device, but make it a derived output + reactive reattach.** Minimal change: one producer emits the device, and an Incus-events watcher re-asserts it on every container `start`. Still uses forkproxy, just stops it silently dying.

These are genuinely different directions, so I want your call rather than guess a fourth time.

# Requirements — netmaker-appliance-nested-blob

## Context

The netmaker stack today is a multi-container `incus-compose` deployment
(`deploy/netmaker/incus-compose.yaml`): `netmaker`, `mq`, `netmaker-ui`,
`prometheus`, `grafana`, and an exporter, each a separate Incus container that
comes up with a default NIC and then has the NIC stripped by `install.sh`.
Mosquitto is the MQTT broker; `deploy/netmaker/rumqttd.toml` carries a stale
comment describing a **host** broker that "replaces the no-NIC netmaker-mq
container." The `netmaker` plugin (`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/netmaker.rs`)
is host-oriented: it checks whether `netclient` is installed on the host, whether
the daemon runs under s6, reads/writes a host `netclient` config path, and
join/leave operate against a host-installed `netclient`.

The target is different and simpler:

- **One self-contained Incus container**, treated as bare metal, holds the
  entire stack: `netmaker` server, **`netclient`**, and **EMQX** (replacing
  Mosquitto), plus supporting services.
- **`systemd` owns those services *inside* the container.** The host stays
  Artix/s6; `s6d` supervises the container as a single unit. Two nested init
  domains — this does not violate the "s6, not systemd" host rule.
- **Host ↔ container is gRPC over Unix domain sockets only** — no NIC, no IP,
  no REST/MQTT leaking to the host. The existing gRPC bridge already carries
  some reflection recognition of container-internal services.
- The whole appliance is expressed as **one nested plugin schema**, sealed as a
  **self-describing btrfs-image blob**, and **activated by loop-mounting** that
  image: its `/blobs` subvolumes feed the reflection catalog and its `/rootfs`
  subvolume is the container's root filesystem. Register = seal, deregister =
  remove, exactly per the blob invariant.

This is the natural end-state of the existing architecture, not a new one. The
blob-as-mountable-btrfs-image primitive already exists
(`crates/op-blob/src/btrfs.rs`); the genuinely new work is the **nested/composite
schema aggregation** and the **`/rootfs` subvolume** extension of the image.

---

## Ground Truth (verified 2026-07-06)

**Already present (do not rebuild):**

- `op-blob/src/btrfs.rs::seal_blobs_into_btrfs_image` seals a set of sealed
  `.blob` files into a btrfs image via `mkfs.btrfs --rootdir --shrink`
  (no mount, no root), one subvolume per plugin, writes `/blob-index.json`,
  verifies the superblock magic, and returns a `mount -o loop,ro` hint. The
  file's own docstring states the goal: a "complete deployment unit …
  mountable (loop/ro), snapshottable, `btrfs send/receive`-able, and
  self-describing."
- `op-blob/src/catalog.rs`: per-object shm layout
  `/dev/shm/opdbus/plugin-blobs/<plugin_id>.<schema_hash16>.blob`;
  `catalog_hash` is a blake3 leaf-fold computed in exactly one place; consumers
  never re-hash. Runtime consumption stays on tmpfs (REQ-8.3: "never
  Btrfs-backed I/O") — the btrfs image is the at-rest/transport form.
- `op-blob/src/blob.rs`: deterministic sealed byte format `OPBLOB01` with
  sections (1 canonical `PluginSchema` JSON, 2 `BlobManifest`, 3
  `FileDescriptorSet`, 4 meta); `BlobManifest` couples schema/D-Bus/gRPC/
  descriptor identity and carries per-method `subid`, `required_capability`,
  `side_effect`, `idempotent`.
- **Nesting is native and already end-to-end.** `op-blob/src/adapter.rs`
  resolves `$defs`/`definitions` inline so nested structs expand;
  `op-blob/src/descriptor.rs` builds nested proto messages from the same defs.
  Both are sealed into the blob (schema-JSON section 1 + descriptor-set section
  3), and the `schema_renderer` / `json_render` plugins render them. So a
  composite appliance state struct that *nests* the child capability structs
  exports its `$defs` into the blob and is rendered by the renderer with no new
  aggregation machinery. There is **no** "subid carry-up gap": the adapter
  intentionally ingests only top-level subids into the uniqueness map, and
  nested-section subids follow the existing plugin-scoped
  `op_blob::inject_common_subids` pattern (a fixed subid baked into a shared
  nested struct would collide globally).

**The real gap:**

- The btrfs image holds only `.blob` control-plane artifacts today; it has **no
  `/rootfs`** subvolume for a bootable container filesystem.
- `netmaker.rs` assumes a **host** `netclient` under s6; it has no notion of a
  container-internal, systemd-owned stack driven over UDS/gRPC.

---

## Functional Requirements

### REQ-1 — One Self-Contained Appliance Container

**REQ-1.1** The netmaker stack MUST collapse into a single Incus container that
holds `netmaker`, `netclient`, and EMQX (and supporting services), treated as
bare metal. The multi-container `incus-compose` topology
(`netmaker`/`mq`/`netmaker-ui`/`prometheus`/`grafana`/exporter as separate
containers) MUST be replaced by this single unit.

**REQ-1.2** `systemd` inside the container owns the internal services. No
internal service may depend on the host init. The host control plane remains
s6; `s6d` supervises the container as one opaque unit (up/down via Incus).

**REQ-1.3** `netclient` MUST run **inside** the container. No host-installed
`netclient` may be required. The `netmaker.rs` fields that assume a host
`netclient` (`installed`, `daemon_running` under s6, host `control_socket`
path) MUST be re-defined against the container-internal, systemd-owned service.

**REQ-1.4** EMQX replaces Mosquitto as the MQTT broker **software only**. The
no-NIC + UDS transport model is unchanged. The stale `rumqttd.toml`
"host broker replaces the no-NIC container" narrative MUST be removed; there is
no host broker and no host `netclient` in this design.

### REQ-2 — gRPC-Only, No NIC, UDS Transport

**REQ-2.1** All host ↔ container I/O (management and data) MUST ride gRPC over
Unix domain sockets. The container MUST have no NIC and no IP for general I/O.

**REQ-2.2** No new `operation.<domain>.v1` proto service package may be created
for the appliance. The appliance is a **plugin** registered via
`crates/op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs`; its surface is reached through
`PluginService.CallMethod`.

**REQ-2.3** Container-internal service discovery MUST come from the appliance
blob's reflection descriptors / `blob-index.json`, never a hardcoded service
list. The gRPC bridge advertises only what the active appliance blob declares.

**REQ-2.4 — Open Question (OQ-1, WireGuard exception).** `netclient` establishes
a WireGuard interface to join the mesh, but the invariant is "no NIC / all I/O
is UDS," and the WireGuard pubkey is also the identity layer. The spec MUST
record which of the following is intended, because it decides whether
`netclient`-in-container is straightforward or needs a shim:
- **(a)** the WG interface is the allowed exception (it is the zero-trust
  identity fabric, not general I/O); `netclient` brings it up internally and
  management/data still ride UDS+gRPC; **or**
- **(b)** even mesh membership is brokered so the container has zero kernel
  network interfaces.
This requirement is **not resolved by this spec**; it is flagged for the owner.

### REQ-3 — Nested / Composite Appliance Schema

**REQ-3.1** The appliance MUST be one addressable D-Bus object
(`/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<appliance>`), i.e. one `plugin_id`, one deterministic
`schema_hash16`, one blob in the catalog.

**REQ-3.2** The appliance state struct MUST nest the child capability structs
(`netmaker`, `netclient`, `emqx`, and any supporting service). schemars emits
their `$defs`; `op-blob/src/adapter.rs` inlines them and `descriptor.rs` builds
the nested proto messages, so the child shapes are exported into the blob and
rendered by the `schema_renderer` / `json_render` plugins — the native path, no
bespoke aggregation. Subids follow the existing plugin-scoped injection
(`op_blob::inject_common_subids`); nested-section fields deliberately stay out
of the top-level uniqueness map (a shared nested struct's fixed subid would
collide globally).

**REQ-3.3** Aggregation MUST be deterministic and computed in exactly one
place (one-schema rule): the same child schemas produce the same appliance
`schema_hash`. No timestamps, sorted maps.

**REQ-3.4** `mut.*` methods on child capabilities MUST retain `actor_id` +
`capability_id`; `evt.*` MUST retain `event_id`/`event_hash` after aggregation.
Every new subid introduced by the appliance is registered in
`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/oscal_subid_registry.rs` (CI-enforced
uniqueness).

**REQ-3.5 — Resolved (composite via native nesting).** The appliance is one
composite plugin whose state struct nests the child structs; `$defs` are
exported into the blob and rendered by the renderer (per Ground Truth). This is
**not** an open question — there is no separate "aggregate bundle" path to weigh,
because native `$defs` nesting already yields one plugin_id / one blob / one
rendered surface.

### REQ-4 — Appliance Blob With `/rootfs` Subvolume

**REQ-4.1** The at-rest appliance artifact MUST be a single btrfs image produced
through the existing `seal_blobs_into_btrfs_image` path (extended), containing:
- `/blobs/<plugin_id>/…` — the sealed schema/descriptor control-plane blobs
  (as today), and
- **`/rootfs`** — a subvolume holding the bootable container filesystem
  (`netmaker` + `netclient` + EMQX binaries, systemd units, configs).

**REQ-4.2** Sealing MUST stay mountless and root-free where the existing path is
(`mkfs.btrfs --rootdir --shrink`). Determinism MUST be preserved: the same
rootfs staging + same blobs produce byte-identical images (sorted, no
timestamps) as far as `mkfs.btrfs` allows; any unavoidable non-determinism MUST
be documented.

**REQ-4.3** Activation ("mount the blob") MUST loop-mount the image read-only,
load the reflection catalog from `/blobs`, and present `/rootfs` as the Incus
container root. Runtime plugin consumption stays on tmpfs (REQ-8.3); the btrfs
image is the at-rest/transport form.

**REQ-4.4** The image MUST remain self-describing, snapshottable, and
`btrfs send/receive`-able (the btrfs.rs stated goal). `/blob-index.json` MUST be
extended to record the `/rootfs` subvolume and the appliance identity.

### REQ-5 — Lifecycle: Register = Seal, Deregister = Remove

**REQ-5.1** Registering the appliance MUST seal it (schema + rootfs) into the
image and place its control-plane blob(s) in the catalog. The appliance exists
⟺ its blob is in the catalog.

**REQ-5.2** Deregistering MUST remove the blob(s) from the catalog and stop the
container as one unit. No orphaned host services, no lingering NIC.

**REQ-5.3** The sole writer of catalog blobs remains the blob sealer in
`op-blob`. SchemaEngine (`op-projection`) only reports the published catalog
hash — it never writes appliance blobs.

### REQ-6 — Reactive, Durable, No Polling

**REQ-6.1** No polling loops or D-Bus watchers in appliance plugin/service code.
State transitions are reactive (arrival-triggered / mutation-triggered).

**REQ-6.2** Durability is the per-mutation immutable chain (`op-blockchain`).
No SQL for state; no snapshot backups of appliance state beyond the blob's own
snapshot/`send`-`receive` capability.

### REQ-7 — Deprecations / Cleanup

**REQ-7.1** `deploy/netmaker/incus-compose.yaml`, `compose.yaml`,
`mosquitto.conf`, `host-mosquitto.conf`, and the stale `rumqttd.toml` narrative
MUST be reconciled with the single-container design (removed or rewritten). No
document may keep describing a host broker or a host `netclient`.

**REQ-7.2** `netmaker.rs` host-`netclient` code paths MUST be removed or
retargeted to the container-internal, UDS/gRPC-driven service per REQ-1.3.

---

## Non-Functional Requirements

**NFR-1 (build/gates).** `cargo check -p op-blob`, `-p op-plugins`,
`-p op-grpc-bridge` MUST be green after each phase; `cargo clippy --workspace
--all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
green at the end.

**NFR-2 (size/RAM).** A bootable `/rootfs` is far larger than a schema blob. It
MUST live only in the loop-mounted btrfs image, never in `/dev/shm`. The tmpfs
catalog materializes only schema/descriptor bytes.

**NFR-3 (Rust-first).** No new Python. `anyhow`/`thiserror`, `simd_json`
preferred. No `Command::new` in plugin/service code except the already-blessed
`mkfs.btrfs` sealing path and bootstrap scripts.

**NFR-4 (subids).** Every new method/surface carries a subid per the taxonomy
and is registered in `oscal_subid_registry.rs`.

---

## Out of Scope

- Frontend / UI work (handled separately by lovable).
- The btrfs *inside* ordinary plugin blobs treated as unmounted subvolumes —
  that is the btrfs control-panel view, explicitly the lowest priority and not
  part of this appliance work.
- Resolving OQ-1 (WireGuard exception) — recorded for the owner; design.md gives
  a recommendation only. (OQ-2 is resolved: composite via native `$defs`
  nesting, REQ-3.5.)

# Tasks — netmaker-appliance-nested-blob

Each task ends with a green gate. Rust gates: `cargo check -p <crate>` (fast),
`cargo clippy … -D warnings` + `cargo fmt --all -- --check` at phase ends.
Phases are ordered so the two open questions are resolved before the expensive
work; nothing here touches the frontend.

---

## Phase 0 — Confirm the two open questions (no code)

### Task 0.1 — Resolve OQ-2 (composite vs bundle) and OQ-1 (WireGuard)
**Requirements**: REQ-3.5, REQ-2.4
**Steps**:
1. Owner confirms the **hybrid composite** recommendation (one appliance

2. Owner confirms **OQ-1(a)** (WG interface is the identity-fabric exception) or

---

## Phase 1 — Nested schema aggregation (control-plane identity)

### Task 1.1 — `compose_appliance_schema` + subid carry-up

**Steps**:

4. Unit test: sorted determinism — same children → identical canonical JSON →

5. Unit test: a child `mut.*`/`evt.*`/`exp.*` subid appears in the composed

**Gate**: `cargo test -p op-plugins appliance::` green.

### Task 1.2 — Register appliance subids
**Requirements**: REQ-3.4, NFR-4
**Steps**:
1. Add appliance-level subids (e.g. `obs.service.netmaker-appliance.status@v1`,
   `mut.service.netmaker-appliance.snapshot@v1`,
   `exp.service.netmaker-appliance.render@v1`) to
   `oscal_subid_registry.rs`.
2. Run the CI subid-uniqueness check.
**Gate**: subid uniqueness test green; `cargo check -p op-plugins` green.

---

## Phase 2 — `/rootfs` extension of the btrfs image

### Task 2.1 — Extend sealing with a `rootfs` subvolume
**Requirements**: REQ-4.1, REQ-4.2, REQ-4.4, NFR-2
**Steps**:
1. In `op-blob/src/btrfs.rs`, add `seal_appliance_image(blob_paths, rootfs_dir,
   appliance_id, image_path)` (or extend the existing fn) that stages `rootfs/`
   next to `blobs/` and passes `--subvol rootfs` to `mkfs.btrfs`.
2. Extend `blob-index.json` to `opdbus-blob-image/2` with `appliance` +
   `rootfs` entries; keep `blobs` backward-compatible.
3. Return `ApplianceImageReport { base, has_rootfs, appliance_id, rootfs_subvol }`.
4. Keep sealing mountless/root-free; document any fs-UUID non-determinism
   (REQ-4.2), pin the UUID if feasible.
5. Unit test with a tiny fake `rootfs/` (a couple of files): superblock magic
   verified, index v2 parses, `has_rootfs == true`.
**Gate**: `cargo test -p op-blob btrfs::` green (skips cleanly if `mkfs.btrfs`
absent, matching existing `which_mkfs` guard).

### Task 2.2 — Activation helper (loop-mount → catalog + rootfs)
**Requirements**: REQ-4.3, REQ-5.1, NFR-2
**Steps**:
1. Add an activation helper that loop-mounts the image ro, loads `/blobs` into
   `ActiveReflectionCatalog` (tmpfs stays authoritative for runtime), and
   returns the `/rootfs` subvol path for Incus.
2. Ensure `/rootfs` is never copied into `/dev/shm` (NFR-2).
**Gate**: `cargo check -p op-blob` green; helper documented with the mount hint.

---

## Phase 3 — Appliance plugin + bridge wiring

### Task 3.1 — `netmaker_appliance` composite plugin
**Requirements**: REQ-1.1, REQ-2.2, REQ-3.1, REQ-6.1
**Steps**:
1. Add `appliance/netmaker_appliance.rs` composing `netmaker`, `netclient`,
   `emqx` via Task 1.1; register it in `default_registry.rs`.
2. Dispatch namespaced methods through the container-internal gRPC endpoint over
   UDS; no polling/watchers.
**Gate**: `cargo check -p op-plugins` green; appliance appears in `ListPlugins`.

### Task 3.2 — Retarget `netmaker.rs` off host-`netclient`
**Requirements**: REQ-1.3, REQ-7.2
**Steps**:
1. Remove/redefine host-`netclient` fields and code paths
   (`installed`/`daemon_running`-under-s6/host `control_socket`,
   `check_netclient_installed`, host config read/write, host `restart_netclient`).
2. Point capability at the container-internal, systemd-owned service.
**Gate**: `cargo check -p op-plugins` green; no host `Command::new` for
`netclient` remains (grep clean).

### Task 3.3 — Bridge reflection from the appliance blob
**Requirements**: REQ-2.1, REQ-2.3
**Steps**:
1. In `op-grpc-bridge`, advertise appliance services from the appliance blob's
   descriptor set (not a static list); reuse existing container-internal
   reflection recognition.
2. Review `grpc_client.rs::netmaker_*`; if it bypasses `CallMethod`, retarget it
   through the plugin surface (no new proto package).
**Gate**: `cargo check -p op-grpc-bridge` green.

---

## Phase 4 — Single-container deploy + cleanup

### Task 4.1 — Single-container appliance build
**Requirements**: REQ-1.1, REQ-1.2, REQ-1.4
**Steps**:
1. Add `deploy/netmaker/appliance/` producing the `rootfs/` staging:
   `netmaker` + `netclient` + `emqx` binaries, `systemd` units, EMQX + netclient
   configs. Bootstrap scripts only (the blessed exception).
2. Wire the staging into `seal_appliance_image` (Task 2.1).
**Gate**: image builds; `verify_btrfs_image` true; `blob-index.json` v2 valid.

### Task 4.2 — Remove stale multi-container / host-broker artifacts
**Requirements**: REQ-1.4, REQ-7.1
**Steps**:
1. Remove/replace `incus-compose.yaml`, `compose.yaml`, `mosquitto.conf`,
   `host-mosquitto.conf`; delete the stale host-broker `rumqttd.toml` narrative.
2. Grep the repo for "host broker" / host-`netclient` docs and reconcile.
**Gate**: `grep -rn "replaces the no-NIC" deploy/` empty; no doc describes a
host broker or host `netclient`.

---

## Phase 5 — (conditional) OQ-1(b) zero-NIC mesh shim
Only if the owner chose OQ-1(b) in Task 0.1. Adds a brokered mesh-membership
path so the container has zero kernel network interfaces. Deferred by default.

---

## Phase 6 — Final audit
**Requirements**: REQ-2.2, REQ-3.3, REQ-5.3, NFR-1
**Steps**:
1. `grep -rn "operation\..*\.v1" crates/` — no new appliance service package.
2. Confirm appliance `schema_hash` is stable across two builds (determinism).
3. Confirm the blob sealer in `op-blob` is the only writer of catalog blobs
   (SchemaEngine only reports the hash).
4. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` and
   `cargo fmt --all -- --check` green.
**Gate**: all above green; both open questions recorded as resolved.

## Context

The netmaker stack today is a multi-container `incus-compose` deployment
(`deploy/netmaker/incus-compose.yaml`): `netmaker`, `mq`, `netmaker-ui`,
`prometheus`, `grafana`, and an exporter, each a separate Incus container that
comes up with a default NIC and then has the NIC stripped by `install.sh`.
Mosquitto is the MQTT broker; `deploy/netmaker/rumqttd.toml` carries a stale
comment describing a **host** broker that "replaces the no-NIC netmaker-mq
container." The `netmaker` plugin (`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/netmaker.rs`)
is host-oriented: it checks whether `netclient` is installed on the host, whether
the daemon runs under s6, reads/writes a host `netclient` config path, and
join/leave operate against a host-installed `netclient`.

The target is different and simpler:

- **One self-contained Incus container**, treated as bare metal, holds the
  entire stack: `netmaker` server, **`netclient`**, and **EMQX** (replacing
  Mosquitto), plus supporting services.
- **`systemd` owns those services *inside* the container.** The host stays
  Artix/s6; `s6d` supervises the container as a single unit. Two nested init
  domains — this does not violate the "s6, not systemd" host rule.
- **Host ↔ container is gRPC over Unix domain sockets only** — no NIC, no IP,
  no REST/MQTT leaking to the host. The existing gRPC bridge already carries
  some reflection recognition of container-internal services.
- The whole appliance is expressed as **one nested plugin schema**, sealed as a
  **self-describing btrfs-image blob**, and **activated by loop-mounting** that
  image: its `/blobs` subvolumes feed the reflection catalog and its `/rootfs`
  subvolume is the container's root filesystem. Register = seal, deregister =
  remove, exactly per the blob invariant.

This is the natural end-state of the existing architecture, not a new one. The
blob-as-mountable-btrfs-image primitive already exists
(`crates/op-blob/src/btrfs.rs`); the genuinely new work is the **nested/composite
schema aggregation** and the **`/rootfs` subvolume** extension of the image.

## Context

The `deploy/netmaker/incus-compose.yaml` (docker-image, multi-container:
`netmaker`, `mq`, `netmaker-ui`, `prometheus`, `grafana`, exporter) is **legacy
and stale** — it does not reflect the current build. netmaker, netclient, and
EMQX are **built from source** and run directly under systemd in **one
bare-metal-like Incus container** (no docker images, no nested containers). The
`netmaker` plugin (`crates/op-plugins/src/state_plugins/netmaker.rs`) is still
host-oriented: it checks whether `netclient` is installed on the host, whether
the daemon runs under s6, reads/writes a host `netclient` config path, and
join/leave operate against a host-installed `netclient` — that is the mismatch
to fix.

The target:

- **One self-contained, bare-metal-like Incus container** holds the entire
  stack: `netmaker` server, **`netclient`**, and **EMQX** (replacing Mosquitto),
  all **built from source**. No nested containers, no docker.
- **`systemd` owns those services *inside* the container.** The host stays
  Artix/s6; `s6d` supervises the container as a single unit. Two nested init
  domains — this does not violate the "s6, not systemd" host rule.
- **Internal interface = netmaker's native REST backend** (`REST_BACKEND=on`).
  The web GUI (`netmaker-ui`) and the reverse proxy are **dropped** — just REST.
- **Host ↔ container control plane is gRPC over a Unix domain socket only** — no
  NIC, no IP, no REST/MQTT leaking to the host. The existing gRPC bridge already
  carries some reflection recognition of container-internal services.
- The gRPC **socket is durable by construction**: it lives inside the
  loop-mounted rootfs blob, so it is present whenever the appliance is mounted —
  no Incus proxy device (forkproxy), no out-of-band bind-mount, no watcher/poll
  to repair it.
- A **network manager built from source** (`rust-network-mgr`) is sealed
  **inside the appliance blob** to own that durable socket and the
  in-container WireGuard/nftables data plane. Because it is in the blob, its
  dependency tree is resolved once at seal time.
- The whole appliance is expressed as **one nested plugin schema**, sealed as a
  **self-describing btrfs-image blob**, and **activated by loop-mounting** that
  image: its `/blobs` subvolumes feed the reflection catalog and its `/rootfs`
  subvolume is the container's root filesystem (and carries the durable socket).
  Register = seal, deregister = remove, exactly per the blob invariant.

This is the natural end-state of the existing architecture, not a new one. The
blob-as-mountable-btrfs-image primitive already exists
(`crates/op-blob/src/btrfs.rs`) and `$defs` nesting is native (see Ground
Truth); the genuinely new work is the **`/rootfs` subvolume** extension of the
image and sealing the from-source stack (netmaker/netclient/EMQX +
network-manager) into it.

(the real network exists only *inside* the appliance; the host control plane
stays IP-free). Its dependency tree MUST be resolved at seal time only — no
per-host dependency resolution at activation. This capability is scoped to the
appliance interior; it MUST NOT introduce IP/nftables logic on the host control
plane.

Because the durable socket dir (`/run/opdbus/`) is *part of `/rootfs`*, step 2
delivers the socket automatically: mounting the subvolume as the container root
makes the socket present. There is no `proxy` device and no bind-mount device to
attach, so nothing can silently fail to "stick," and no watcher is needed to
re-assert it (REQ-2.5 / REQ-6.1).

---

## Component 2b — Durable socket + in-appliance network manager (`rust-network-mgr`)

The "hit or miss whether the plugin sticks to the container" failure came from
delivering the socket as a separate Incus device (proxy/forkproxy) reconciled by
a different owner than the socket binder — two uncoordinated timelines, plus a
flaky forkproxy. This design removes the device entirely:

- **The socket is an artifact of the rootfs blob**, not a device. It binds
  inside the container (systemd-owned `rust-network-mgr`, built from source,
  holds the `UnixListener` for its lifetime — the same durable-listener pattern
  the existing `unix_socket`/`shared_unix_socket` plugins use). Its path lives
  under `/run/opdbus/` inside `/rootfs`, so present-state = the mount.
- **`rust-network-mgr` is sealed inside the appliance blob** (REQ-2.6). Its real
  capability (rtnetlink → nftables) is legitimate *here* because the appliance
  interior has a real network: netclient's WireGuard interface + the netmaker
  mesh. It manages that interior data plane and owns the durable socket. Its
  dependency tree is resolved once, at seal.
- **Host invariant intact.** None of this puts IP/nftables on the host control
  plane; the host still sees only the one gRPC/UDS surface. `rust-network-mgr`'s
  own extras (its axum REST port, its stdio MCP binary, its text control socket)
  are **not** exposed — only the durable gRPC socket crosses the boundary.

> This is why `rust-network-mgr` is the piece worth keeping: not its
> nftables/Docker code for the host, but a from-source, blob-sealable owner of a
> durable in-appliance socket + WG/nftables interior.

**Requirements**: REQ-3.1, REQ-3.2, REQ-3.3, REQ-3.4

3. Apply appliance-level subids on the nested fields; run
   `op_blob::inject_common_subids` for shared nested-section subids — do NOT add

# Design — netmaker-appliance-nested-blob

## Goal

Collapse the whole netmaker stack into **one self-contained Incus container**
(systemd-owned internally, no NIC, UDS/gRPC only), describe it as **one nested
plugin schema**, seal it as **one self-describing btrfs-image blob** that carries
both the control-plane `.blob`s and the bootable `/rootfs`, and **activate it by
loop-mounting** that image. Register = seal, deregister = remove.

```
        ┌──────────────────────── HOST (Artix / s6) ────────────────────────┐
        │  s6d supervises the appliance as ONE unit (incus up/down)          │
        │                                                                    │
        │  op-grpc-bridge ──UDS──▶ appliance gRPC endpoint                   │
        │        ▲                        │                                  │
        │        │ reflection from        │ CallMethod{plugin_id, method}    │
        │        │ appliance blob         ▼                                  │
        │  ActiveReflectionCatalog   ┌───────────────────────────────────┐  │
        │  (tmpfs /dev/shm)          │  INCUS CONTAINER  (bare-metal-like)│  │
        │        ▲ loads /blobs      │  root = /rootfs subvolume (loop-ro)│  │
        │        │                   │  systemd owns:                     │  │
        │  ┌─────┴───────────────┐   │    • netmaker (server)             │  │
        │  │ appliance btrfs img │   │    • netclient  (OQ-1: wg iface)   │  │
        │  │  /blobs/<id>/*.blob │   │    • emqx  (MQTT, replaces mosq.)  │  │
        │  │  /rootfs (bootable) │   │    • exporters / supporting svcs   │  │
        │  │  /blob-index.json   │   │  all inter-service comms LOCAL     │  │
        │  └─────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────────────┘  │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

No NIC on the container; the only external surface is the UDS the bridge dials.
The WireGuard interface (if OQ-1(a)) is the identity fabric, not general I/O.

---

## Nesting is native (was OQ-2 — resolved)

---

## Determinism & durability

- Appliance `schema_hash` is deterministic over the composite JSON (sorted, no
  timestamps) — the artifact identity in `<plugin_id>.<hash16>.blob`.
- Image byte-determinism is best-effort per REQ-4.2; the schema-blob layer is
  fully deterministic regardless of the rootfs.
- Durability = `op-blockchain` per-mutation chain + btrfs snapshot /
  `send`/`receive`. No SQL for state; no separate snapshot backups.

## What is explicitly NOT changed

- The tmpfs runtime catalog and `catalog_hash` computation (one-schema rule).
- The sealed `OPBLOB01` byte format and section layout.
- Host s6 supervision model; only the *container internals* use systemd.
- Frontend (lovable).

content.text:
Right - the sealed blob is `mount -o loop,ro` (immutable by design, that's what makes it deterministic and hashable), so netmaker/EMQX/netclient can't boot directly on it: they need writable `/run`, `/var/lib/{netmaker,emqx,netclient}`, sqlite, WG keys, logs. So yes, you need a writable layer. Let me lay out what's real, because one part of the idea can't work as stated.

## The blob can't hold the persistent layer *inside* itself
The image is one loop file mounted `ro`. A subvolume inside a `ro` block device is also `ro` - you can't write to it without mounting the whole image `rw`, which breaks immutability/determinism. So the persistent writable layer must be a **separate** writable btrfs subvolume (it can sit right next to the blob, but not inside the sealed ro image). The blob stays the immutable *definition*; the writable subvolume is the *instance*.

## Three tiers, not two
1. **Immutable base** - sealed blob `/rootfs`, `loop,ro`. Deterministic, hashed. (the definition)
2. **Persistent state** - a writable btrfs subvolume: netclient WG keys, netmaker sqlite, EMQX data. Survives restart, snapshotable.
3. **Ephemeral runtime** - tmpfs: `/run`, `/tmp`, caches. Wiped on stop.

## How to get the writable layer - three mechanisms
- **Incus-native btrfs CoW (least new code).** Import the blob's `/rootfs` subvolume as an Incus base image on a btrfs storage pool; Incus *already* snapshots it into a writable per-instance rootfs (native btrfs CoW). That IS your runtime/persistent separation - no overlayfs, no hand-rolling. Blob stays the immutable seed; activation = `btrfs receive`/import into the pool. This is basically the layered-btrfs you described, done by Incus.
- **overlayfs "volatile overlay".** `lowerdir` = loop,ro blob rootfs; `upperdir` = tmpfs (ephemeral) plus a persistent btrfs subvolume for state. Works without Incus's storage pool, but you manage whiteouts/layers yourself.
- **btrfs receive + snapshot (fully native, no overlay).** `btrfs receive` the rootfs subvol into a rw pool once, then `btrfs subvolume snapshot` per boot. Cleanest CoW + rollback, but needs a rw pool and a restore step (not mountless-ro).

## On "ditch the Incus container"
Honest take: Incus isn't just a rootfs holder - it provides the namespacing (mount/pid/user-ns idmap), cgroups, and lifecycle. On an s6 host (no systemd) you can't use `systemd-nspawn`, so ditching Incus means rebuilding a container runtime (crun/runc under s6) to boot a systemd-PID1 rootfs. And Incus's btrfs pool is *already* the CoW layering you want. So dropping Incus costs you more than the layer saves - the better move is to keep Incus but make its rootfs the blob's btrfs subvolume, so Incus does the CoW and you keep one immutable definition.

## One open question this exposes
Where does the appliance's **identity** (netclient WG keypair, netmaker sqlite) live? If it's generated at first boot into the persistent subvolume, the instance is stateful and not reproducible from the blob alone. Either (a) the persistent subvolume is the identity anchor (snapshot it for durability), or (b) identity is provisioned into the blob at seal (makes each blob instance-specific). This ties into OQ-1 (WG identity).

## The model (generalizes to all user containers)
1. **One golden base** - immutable btrfs subvolume / sealed blob rootfs, made **once** (your "snapshot to base all containers off of"), shared `ro` lowerdir. No per-instance snapshots, so no maintenance.
2. **Per-container upper = tmpfs** - ephemeral runtime, wiped on stop. Overlay merge = the container root.

4. **Persistence = soul + namespaced memory in CozoDB** (op-cognitive-mcp), keyed by that identity. This is the durable layer, not the filesystem.

## Why it fits every invariant
- "no SQL for state; graph store is CozoDB" → persistence is the CozoDB soul/namespace, not container-disk sqlite.
- "a container's name IS its sessionid" → identity from keypair, ✓.
- "the sealed blob IS the plugin" → golden base is the immutable definition, ✓.
- Reactive/no-poll → fs is ephemeral, memory is queried not synced, ✓.

It can't live only in memory-graph and it must not be left on the ephemeral fs - it's **injected at boot from the identity store**, iface brought up, never written to the overlay. Worth confirming where op-identity custodies the privkey vs just the pubkey.
3. **tmpfs = RAM.** Heavy writers (EMQX retained msgs) in tmpfs cost memory - fine only because real state is offloaded to CozoDB.

info:
 description: \|-
 # API Usage

 Most actions that can be performed via API can be performed via UI. We recommend managing your networks using the official netmaker-ui project. However, Netmaker can also be run without the UI, and all functions can be achieved via API calls. If your use case requires using Netmaker without the UI or you need to do some troubleshooting/advanced configuration, using the API directly may help.

 # Authentication

 API calls must be authenticated via a header of the format -H “Authorization: Bearer ” There are two methods to obtain YOUR\_SECRET\_KEY: 1. Using the masterkey. By default, this value is “secret key,” but you should change this on your instance and keep it secure. This value can be set via env var at startup or in a config file (config/environments/< env >.yaml). See the \[Netmaker\](https://docs.netmaker.org/index.html) documentation for more details. 2. Using a JWT received for a node. This can be retrieved by calling the /api/nodes//authenticate endpoint, as documented below.

## Component 3 — Appliance plugin surface (`op-plugins`)

Replace the host-oriented `netmaker.rs` internals (REQ-7.2) with a
container-internal driver reached over UDS. The plugin's `apply_state` /
method dispatch talks to the container's internal gRPC endpoint (or the
systemd-managed services via that endpoint), never a host `netclient`.

Authoritative Method → child → transport table:

| Appliance method            | Child      | Effect (inside container)                    | subid category |
|---|---|---|---|
| `netmaker.join_network`     | netmaker   | server-side network join                     | `mut`          |
| `netmaker.leave_network`    | netmaker   | server-side leave                            | `mut`          |
| `netmaker.list_networks`    | netmaker   | read networks                                | `obs`          |
| `netclient.status`          | netclient  | wg/mesh status (OQ-1)                         | `obs`          |
| `netclient.restart`         | netclient  | restart internal systemd unit                | `mut`          |
| `emqx.list_clients`         | emqx       | broker client list                           | `obs`          |
| `emqx.get_stats`            | emqx       | broker metrics                               | `obs`          |
| `appliance.status`          | appliance  | aggregate health of all internal units       | `obs`          |
| `appliance.snapshot`        | appliance  | `btrfs send`-able image snapshot             | `mut`          |

Method names, subids, and `required_capability` come from the composite schema
(single source of truth); the table restates them for review, it does not add
them independently.

### Core Functional Requirements

[Permalink: Core Functional Requirements](https://github.com/sparesparrow/rust-network-mgr#core-functional-requirements)

1. **IP Address Monitoring:** Detect interface IP additions/removals via Netlink.
2. **Atomic NFTables Set Updates:** Reliably update configured `nftables` sets (e.g., `inet filter/wan_ips`) when corresponding interface IPs change. Uses `rustables` for atomic updates.
3. **Configuration Parsing:** Load interface configurations specifying DHCP status, static addresses (optional), and the target `nftables_zone`.
4. **Socket Control:** Accept `reload`, `status`, `ping` commands.
5. **(Optional) Docker IP Tracking:** Maintain an internal map of running container IDs to their discovered IP addresses.

### NFTables Setup Example

This service *expects* a base `nftables` configuration to exist. It only manages the *elements* within predefined sets.

Example base `/etc/nftables.conf` snippet:

```nftables
table inet filter {
    set wan_ips {
        type ipv4_addr
        flags dynamic
    }
    set lan_ips {
        type ipv4_addr
        flags dynamic
    }

    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy accept;

        # Example rule using the set
        ip saddr @wan_ips counter drop
    }

    # ... other chains and rules
}
````

### Build, Test, and Run

[Permalink: Build, Test, and Run](https://github.com/sparesparrow/rust-network-mgr#build-test-and-run)

- **Build:**`cargo build --release` (Binary at `target/release/rust-network-mgr`)
- **Test:**`cargo test` (Some tests require `sudo` and `nftables`)

  - Run ignored tests: `sudo cargo test -- --ignored`
- **Lint:**`cargo clippy`
- **Format:**`cargo fmt`
- **Run:**
  - Ensure `/etc/rust-network-mgr/config.yaml` exists or set `RUST_NETWORK_MGR_CONFIG`.
  - **(Docker)** Ensure the service user has permissions for `/var/run/docker.sock` if Docker monitoring is desired.
  - Run directly (requires privileges for Netlink/nftables/Docker): `sudo target/release/rust-network-mgr`
  - Use the example systemd service: Copy `pkg-files/systemd/rust-network-mgr.service` to `/etc/systemd/system/`, then `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, `sudo systemctl start rust-network-mgr`. Check status with `sudo systemctl status rust-network-mgr` and logs with `sudo journalctl -u rust-network-mgr -f`.

## Development Priorities & Scope

[Permalink: Development Priorities & Scope](https://github.com/sparesparrow/rust-network-mgr#development-priorities--scope)

1. **Reliability:** Ensure correct behavior under various network conditions.
2. **Correctness:** Accurately update `nftables` sets based on monitored IPs.
3. **Simplicity:** Maintain a focused scope on coordinating Netlink events with `nftables` set updates. Optional features like Docker monitoring should be self-contained and fail gracefully.
4. **Testability:** Design components for unit and integration testing.

**Current Scope:** This tool focuses primarily on monitoring interface IPs via Netlink and updating _pre-existing_`nftables` sets based on a simple configuration map (`nftables_zone`). It does _not_ manage `nftables` rules, tables, or chains beyond adding/removing IPs from sets. The optional Docker monitoring currently tracks container IPs internally but does not yet integrate them into `nftables` rules.

## Potential Future Features / Roadmap

[Permalink: Potential Future Features / Roadmap](https://github.com/sparesparrow/rust-network-mgr#potential-future-features--roadmap)

While the core focus is narrow, future enhancements could include:

- More sophisticated `nftables` interaction (e.g., managing rules directly).
- IPv6 support in `nftables` sets.
- **Docker Integration Enhancements:**
  - Using discovered container IPs in `nftables` rules/sets (e.g., based on container labels or predefined mappings).
  - Monitoring Docker network attach/detach events for more granular IP tracking.
- More detailed status reporting via the control socket (e.g., listing tracked container IPs).

_(These are ideas, not commitments. Development follows the priorities above.)_

TOOL: TOOL_RESULT: //! Shared Unix Domain Socket — Full Tonic Data Plane
//!
//! Serves the identical gRPC service stack over a single host-side UDS that
//! thousands of containers connect to. Identity is resolved from the peer
//! credentials (via tonic's native `UdsConnectInfo`) and mapped to the
//! canonical Ghostbridge footprint for the same interceptor gating.
//!
//! ## Identity Model
//!
//! ```text
//! Container connects → UDS accept → tonic::UdsConnectInfo.peer_cred
//!   → peer UID/PID as lookup key
//!   → resolve canonical session_id from /dev/shm/plugin_schema.dat
//!   → inject x-ghostbridge-footprint + x-ghostbridge-trace-id
//!   → same GhostbridgeInterceptor applies
//! ```
//!
//! The socket path is configurable via `GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_PATH` env var,
//! defaulting to `/run/ghostbridge/container.sock`.

use std::ffi::CString;
use std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt;
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

use tokio::net::UnixListener;
use tokio_stream::wrappers::UnixListenerStream;
use tonic::transport::server::UdsConnectInfo;
use tracing::info;

/// Default path for the shared container socket.
pub const DEFAULT_SOCKET_PATH: &str = "/run/ghostbridge/container.sock";
const DEFAULT_SOCKET_MODE: u32 = 0o666;

/// Resolved canonical identity from peer credentials.
///
/// This is NOT minted from cgroup names — it is looked up against the
/// authoritative IdentitySled in shared memory. The peer_cred (UID/PID)
/// is the lookup key, not the identity itself.
#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct CanonicalPeerIdentity {
    /// The hex-encoded hashed_footprint from the IdentitySled.
    pub footprint_hex: String,
    /// The hex-encoded trace_id from the IdentitySled.
    pub trace_id_hex: String,
    /// Whether the identity is valid (sled exists and is non-zero).
    pub is_valid: bool,
}

impl CanonicalPeerIdentity {
    /// Resolve the canonical identity from the shared-memory sled.
    ///
    /// For UDS connections, the peer credential is the acceptable anchor
    /// but the identity itself comes from the sled — the same source that
    /// the GhostbridgeInterceptor validates against.
    pub fn from_sled() -> Self {
        match op_identity::read_sled() {
            Ok((sled_ptr, _mmap)) => {
                let sled = unsafe { &*sled_ptr };
                let is_valid = sled.hashed_footprint != [0u8; 32] && sled.trace_id != [0u8; 16];
                Self {
                    footprint_hex: hex::encode(sled.hashed_footprint),
                    trace_id_hex: sled.trace_id_hex(),
                    is_valid,
                }
            }
            Err(_) => Self {
                footprint_hex: String::new(),
                trace_id_hex: String::new(),
                is_valid: false,
            },
        }
    }
}

/// Bind the shared container socket and return a stream suitable for
/// `tonic::transport::Server::serve_with_incoming()`.
///
/// The returned `UnixListenerStream` yields `tokio::net::UnixStream` items
/// that tonic will automatically extract `UdsConnectInfo` (including peer_cred)
/// from via its `Connected` trait implementation.
pub async fn bind_shared_socket() -> std::io::Result<UnixListenerStream> {
    let path = PathBuf::from(
        std::env::var("GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_PATH")
            .unwrap_or_else(|_| DEFAULT_SOCKET_PATH.to_string()),
    );

    // Ensure parent directory exists.
    if let Some(parent) = path.parent() {
        tokio::fs::create_dir_all(parent).await?;
    }

    if let Err(e) = tokio::fs::remove_file(&path).await {
        if e.kind() != std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound {
            return Err(e);
        }
    }

    let listener = UnixListener::bind(&path)?;

    apply_socket_permissions(&path)?;

    info!(socket_path = %path.display(), "Shared container socket bound");

    Ok(UnixListenerStream::new(listener))
}

/// Apply ownership/mode to a freshly bound socket.
///
/// Env:
/// - `GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_UID`: numeric owner uid.
/// - `GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_GID`: numeric owner gid.
/// - `GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_MODE`: octal mode, default `0666`.
pub fn apply_socket_permissions(path: &Path) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    #[cfg(unix)]
    {
        use std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt;

        let uid = parse_env_id("GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_UID")?;
        let gid = parse_env_id("GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_GID")?;

        if uid.is_some() || gid.is_some() {
            let c_path = CString::new(path.as_os_str().as_bytes()).map_err(|_| {
                std::io::Error::new(
                    std::io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput,
                    "socket path contains interior NUL",
                )
            })?;
            let uid = uid.map_or(!0 as libc::uid_t, |value| value as libc::uid_t);
            let gid = gid.map_or(!0 as libc::gid_t, |value| value as libc::gid_t);

            // SAFETY: c_path is NUL-terminated and points to the socket path.
            let result = unsafe { libc::chown(c_path.as_ptr(), uid, gid) };
            if result != 0 {
                return Err(std::io::Error::last_os_error());
            }
        }

        let mode = parse_socket_mode()?;
        std::fs::set_permissions(path, std::fs::Permissions::from_mode(mode))?;
        info!(
            socket_path = %path.display(),
            uid = ?uid,
            gid = ?gid,
            mode = format_args!("{:04o}", mode),
            "Applied shared socket ownership"
        );
    }

    Ok(())
}

#[cfg(unix)]
fn parse_env_id(name: &str) -> std::io::Result<Option<u32>> {
    match std::env::var(name) {
        Ok(value) if value.trim().is_empty() => Ok(None),
        Ok(value) => value.trim().parse::<u32>().map(Some).map_err(|error| {
            std::io::Error::new(
                std::io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput,
                format!("invalid {name}: {error}"),
            )
        }),
        Err(std::env::VarError::NotPresent) => Ok(None),
        Err(error) => Err(std::io::Error::new(
            std::io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput,
            format!("invalid {name}: {error}"),
        )),
    }
}

#[cfg(unix)]
fn parse_socket_mode() -> std::io::Result<u32> {
    let value = match std::env::var("GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_MODE") {
        Ok(value) if !value.trim().is_empty() => value,
        Ok(_) | Err(std::env::VarError::NotPresent) => return Ok(DEFAULT_SOCKET_MODE),
        Err(error) => {
            return Err(std::io::Error::new(
                std::io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput,
                format!("invalid GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_MODE: {error}"),
            ))
        }
    };

    let trimmed = value.trim();
    let octal = trimmed
        .strip_prefix("0o")
        .or_else(|| trimmed.strip_prefix("0O"))
        .unwrap_or(trimmed);
    u32::from_str_radix(octal, 8).map_err(|error| {
        std::io::Error::new(
            std::io::ErrorKind::InvalidInput,
            format!("invalid GHOSTBRIDGE_SOCKET_MODE: {error}"),
        )
    })
}

/// Extract peer credentials from a tonic request's extensions.
///
/// This is available on any request served over the UDS path because tonic
/// automatically populates `UdsConnectInfo` for `UnixStream` connections.
pub fn extract_peer_cred<T>(request: &tonic::Request<T>) -> Option<tokio::net::unix::UCred> {
    request
        .extensions()
        .get::<UdsConnectInfo>()
        .and_then(|info| info.peer_cred)
}

/// UDS identity interceptor.
///
/// For the UDS path, we inject the canonical footprint and trace_id from the
/// sled into the request metadata so the downstream GhostbridgeInterceptor
/// sees the same headers it expects from the Xray/HTTP path.
///
/// This is the UDS equivalent of Xray injecting `X-Ghostbridge-Footprint`.
#[allow(clippy::result_large_err)]
pub fn uds_identity_interceptor(
    mut req: tonic::Request<()>,
) -> Result<tonic::Request<()>, tonic::Status> {
    let identity = CanonicalPeerIdentity::from_sled();

    if !identity.is_valid {
        return Err(tonic::Status::failed_precondition(
            "Identity sled unavailable or invalid — UDS connection rejected",
        ));
    }

    // Inject the canonical footprint so the GhostbridgeInterceptor passes.
    let fp = identity
        .footprint_hex
        .parse::<tonic::metadata::MetadataValue<tonic::metadata::Ascii>>()
        .map_err(|_| tonic::Status::internal("Failed to encode footprint header"))?;
    let tr = identity
        .trace_id_hex
        .parse::<tonic::metadata::MetadataValue<tonic::metadata::Ascii>>()
        .map_err(|_| tonic::Status::internal("Failed to encode trace_id header"))?;

    req.metadata_mut().insert("x-ghostbridge-footprint", fp);
    req.metadata_mut().insert("x-ghostbridge-trace-id", tr);

    Ok(req)
}
